reconcile.connective: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown split the chapiter into a plain tier 2 Kings omits and a carved tier it alone records, so both totals hold.

discrepancy.connective: Keil & Delitzsch concede the "three cubits" reading is corrupt, emending it to "five" to match Jeremiah rather than harmonizing both numbers as transmitted.

excerpts.excerpt_text: five cubits—so Kg1 7:16. But Kg2 25:17 has “three cubits.” There were two parts in the chapiter: the one lower and plain, of two cubits; the other, higher and curiously carved, of three cubits. The former is omitted in Kg2 25:17, as belonging to the shaft of the pillar; the latter alone is there mentioned. Here the whole chapiter of five cubits is referred to.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB names the specific 3-vs-5 cubit conflict between 2 Kings 25:17 and Jeremiah 52:22/1 Kings 7:16 directly and gives the two-tier (plain base + carved crown) explanation for why 2 Kings records only part of the same measurement.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Instead of אמּה שׁלשׁ we must read אמּת המשׁ, five cubits, according to Jer 52:22 and Kg1 7:16.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: K&D concede the "three cubits" reading in 2 Kings 25:17 is itself a corrupted text and explicitly emend it to "five cubits" to match Jeremiah 52:22/1 Kings 7:16, rather than reading the two figures as both accurate as transmitted.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley lists this exact pair — "Chapiter's length, 5 cubits, 1 Kings vii. 16; 3 cubits, 2 Kings xxv. 17" — under his 'confounding of similar numeral letters' explanation for numeral discrepancies (p. 382).
